topics.title: Diverse Perspectives on Justice
topics.benchmark_preservation: The approved design reference, prior topic artifacts and canonical Political Theory owners remain immutable.

panels.panel_title: Perspective Map, Stakes and Essential Vocabulary
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Perspective Map, Stakes and Essential Vocabulary
[1] Gauba presents rival perspectives on justice rather than one settled formula.
v
[2] Rawls, Nozick, Marxism, socialism, anarchism, feminism and communitarianism differ.
v
[3] The topic rewards comparison of rule, state, property, equality and community.
v
[4] A good answer identifies the standard of justice before judging outcomes.
v
VERDICT -> The chapter is comparative by design.
ANSWER USE -> Name the rival standard of justice first.
CENTRAL FOCUS
The Eight-Perspective Chapter Spine
[1] Rawls does not defend simple equality of outcome.
v
[2] Equal basic liberties come first, then fair opportunity, then difference.
v
[3] Original position and veil of ignorance model a fair choice situation.
v
[4] State the ordering clearly before giving objections.
v
VERDICT -> Rawls requires ordered principles, not one slogan.
ANSWER USE -> State liberty, opportunity and difference in sequence.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Rawls, Nozick and Controlling Distinctions
[1] Nozick does not deny justice; he denies patterned redistribution as the master test.
v
[2] Entitlement theory turns on acquisition, transfer and rectification together.
v
[3] Wilt Chamberlain attacks end-state patterning through voluntary exchange.
v
[4] The water-source case shows that acquisition is not morally unlimited.
v
VERDICT -> Nozick's history matters as much as present consent.
ANSWER USE -> Mention rectification when title history is disputed.

panels.panel_title: Thinkers and Rival Standards of Justice
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Thinkers and Rival Standards of Justice
[1] Marxist critique targets exploitation, surplus value and productive control.
v
[2] Democratic socialism keeps social justice but rejects dictatorship.
v
[3] Both are socialist corrections, yet they diverge on freedom and method.
v
[4] Do not collapse welfare constitutionalism into revolutionary centralism.
v
VERDICT -> Socialism divides over freedom, method and state form.
ANSWER USE -> Separate welfare constitutionalism from centralism.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Illustrative Cases and Evidence Units
[1] Anarchist justice begins from suspicion of coercive authority itself.
v
[2] Voluntary cooperation and decentralisation are preferred to imposed hierarchy.
v
[3] Its strength is anti-domination; its weakness is scale and regulation.
v
[4] A serious answer names both without caricaturing anarchism as chaos.
v
VERDICT -> Anarchism critiques domination, not coordination as such.
ANSWER USE -> Balance voluntary order with the scale objection.
CENTRAL FOCUS
The Six-Axis Comparative Matrix
[1] Feminist justice shows that identical treatment can preserve subordination.
v
[2] Corrective support answers unequal burdens in property, work and representation.
v
[3] Subaltern justice asks why marginal groups stay undervalued under elite rule.
v
[4] Both widen justice beyond contract and exchange toward power and voice.
v
VERDICT -> Formal equality can leave structural subordination intact.
ANSWER USE -> Show why correction is not identical treatment.

panels.panel_title: Trap Repair, Boundaries and PYQ Routes
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Trap Repair, Boundaries and PYQ Routes
[1] Gramsci matters here as the hegemony route into subaltern critique.
v
[2] Domination can persist because injustice appears natural or consensual.
v
[3] Justice must test public meaning as well as material reward.
v
[4] Elite-centred history and subordinate agency must remain distinct.
v
VERDICT -> Hegemony explains why injustice can appear normal.
ANSWER USE -> Link subaltern critique to public meaning and reward.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Revision Spine and Directive Control
[1] Communitarian critique begins with the socially embedded self.
v
[2] Complex equality blocks money or power from buying every other good.
v
[3] Community meaning is not a licence for authoritarian conformity.
v
[4] The best answer criticises liberal abstraction without discarding justice.
v
VERDICT -> Community meanings qualify but do not abolish justice.
ANSWER USE -> Use Walzer to block one sphere dominating another.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Argument Reconstruction and Objection-Reply Chains
[1] The safest answer grid is rule, state, property, equality, community and critique.
v
[2] Rawls and Nozick should be compared historically and institutionally.
v
[3] Feminist and subaltern critiques are widening moves, not decorative appendices.
v
[4] Identify the object of justice before choosing the remedy.
v
VERDICT -> The six-axis grid prevents descriptive overflow.
ANSWER USE -> Compare rule, state, property, equality, community and critique.

panels.panel_title: Indian Applications, Quotation Safety and MCQ Ledger
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Indian Applications, Quotation Safety and MCQ Ledger
[1] Capability approach and parity of participation are bounded extensions.
v
[2] Capability asks what persons can actually be and do.
v
[3] Parity asks whether persons can participate as peers without status injury.
v
[4] Tag both as extensions, not as Gauba's own chapter vocabulary.
v
VERDICT -> Supplementary bridges must remain explicitly bounded.
ANSWER USE -> Tag capability and parity as extensions, not Gauba terms.
CENTRAL FOCUS
MCQ Remediation and Trap Repair
[1] Cross-applied verified PYQs remain owned by Philosophy files.
v
[2] Rawls, Nozick, Plato, Sen and Mill route through Social and Political Ideals.
v
[3] Gender, caste and multicultural routes stay with their Philosophy owners.
v
[4] Political Theory borrows those routes without rerouting ownership.
v
VERDICT -> Cross-application never transfers Philosophy ownership.
ANSWER USE -> Keep the original Philosophy owner explicit.
CENTRAL FOCUS
PYQ Ownership and Answer Practice
[1] Indian illustrations here are analytical bridges, not Gauba-sourced doctrine.
v
[2] Do not cite the 44th-Amendment property bridge as Gauba chapter content.
v
[3] Topic 23 owns democratisation, backsliding and social-movement bridges.
v
[4] Topic 20 supplies justice standards later used to judge those processes.
v
VERDICT -> Topic 20 ends where Topic 23's democratic bridges begin.
ANSWER USE -> Route democratisation and backsliding forward to Topic 23.
